report:
**Conclusion:** The claim is not supported by high-quality evidence. Research does **not** show that receiving more childhood vaccines increases autism risk.

A 2014 meta-analysis combining five cohort studies (1.26 million children) and five case-control studies found no association between vaccination and autism/ASD; it also found no association for MMR or thimerosal/mercury exposure. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24814559/

Directly relevant to “more vaccines,” a study of cumulative exposure to vaccine antigens in the first two years of life found that greater exposure was not associated with autism. This is important because vaccine count alone is an imperfect measure of immune exposure: modern vaccines can contain fewer antigens than some older vaccines. The study is cited as DeStefano, Price, and Weintraub (2013), *Journal of Pediatrics*, DOI 10.1016/j.jpeds.2013.02.001. https://www.redalyc.org/journal/582/58257575001/

A large Danish nationwide cohort study likewise found MMR vaccination did not increase autism risk, including in children considered more susceptible or during periods after vaccination. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30831578/

Autism is a neurodevelopmental condition with substantial genetic and multifactorial contributors. Rising diagnoses do not establish that vaccines cause autism; diagnostic criteria, awareness, and access to assessment also affect recorded prevalence.
